entry_schema.purpose: Comprehensive machine-readable explainer preserving definitions, protocol mechanisms, message structures, method semantics, transport relationships, versions, history, security, standards and provenance.
entry_schema.source_fidelity: The uploaded source is authoritative for source-derived content. Expansion targets identify subjects not fully explained by the source rather than silently importing facts.
entry_schema.relationship_policy: Directional relationships preserve mechanism, semantic role, and source provenance where supported.

nodes.label: HTTP
nodes.description: Hypertext Transfer Protocol; an application-layer protocol in the Internet protocol suite for distributed, collaborative, hypermedia information systems.

nodes.label: Hypertext Transfer Protocol
nodes.description: Expanded name of HTTP.

nodes.label: Application layer
nodes.description: Layer in the Internet protocol suite where HTTP operates.

nodes.label: Internet protocol suite
nodes.description: Protocol suite containing HTTP and its underlying transport/network/link layers.

nodes.label: World Wide Web
nodes.description: HTTP is described as the foundation of data communication for the World Wide Web.

nodes.label: Hypertext
nodes.description: Documents containing hyperlinks to other resources.

nodes.label: Hypermedia information systems
nodes.description: Distributed, collaborative systems for hypermedia information.

nodes.label: Client
nodes.description: Participant that submits an HTTP request and receives a response.

nodes.label: Server
nodes.description: Participant that receives HTTP requests and returns HTTP responses.

nodes.label: HTTP request
nodes.description: Message submitted by a client to a server.

nodes.label: HTTP response
nodes.description: Message returned by a server describing disposition and optionally containing a requested resource.

nodes.label: Request-response protocol
nodes.description: HTTP transaction model in which a client request is followed by a server response.

nodes.label: User agent
nodes.description: Software acting on behalf of a user to access, consume, or display web content.

nodes.label: Web browser
nodes.description: Example of a user agent and common HTTP client.

nodes.label: Web server
nodes.description: Server hosting one or more websites and acting as an HTTP server.

nodes.label: Web crawler
nodes.description: Indexing software used by search providers; an HTTP user agent.

nodes.label: Voice browser
nodes.description: Voice-oriented HTTP user agent.

nodes.label: Mobile app
nodes.description: Software that can access, consume, or display web content.

nodes.label: Web resource
nodes.description: Resource addressed and transferred through HTTP.

nodes.label: URL
nodes.description: Uniform Resource Locator used to locate a web resource.

nodes.label: URI
nodes.description: Uniform Resource Identifier; HTTP resources are located through URI schemes http and https.

nodes.label: http URI scheme
nodes.description: URI scheme used for HTTP resources.

nodes.label: https URI scheme
nodes.description: URI scheme used for secure HTTP resources.

nodes.label: HTML
nodes.description: Hypertext markup format used in examples and historically returned by early HTTP.

nodes.label: Hyperlink
nodes.description: Link from one resource/document to another.

nodes.label: Intermediate network element
nodes.description: Network element positioned between clients and servers to improve or enable communication.

nodes.label: Web cache
nodes.description: Intermediate cache that can deliver content on behalf of upstream servers.

nodes.label: Browser cache
nodes.description: Client-side cache for previously accessed web resources.

nodes.label: HTTP proxy
nodes.description: Proxy server that relays HTTP messages between clients and external servers.

nodes.label: Private network boundary
nodes.description: Boundary where a proxy can relay traffic for clients lacking globally routable addresses.

nodes.label: Upstream server
nodes.description: Origin/upstream server on behalf of which a cache may deliver content.

nodes.label: Hop-by-hop header
nodes.description: HTTP header managed by intermediate nodes for each hop.

nodes.label: End-to-end header
nodes.description: HTTP header managed only by source client and target web server.

nodes.label: HTTP/0.9
nodes.description: Early HTTP version; obsolete.

nodes.label: HTTP/1.0
nodes.description: HTTP version finalized in 1996; obsolete.

nodes.label: HTTP/1.1
nodes.description: Standard HTTP version with persistent connections and other enhancements.

nodes.label: HTTP/2
nodes.description: Standard version adding binary representation, multiplexed streams, and other performance features.

nodes.label: HTTP/3
nodes.description: Standard version using QUIC over UDP rather than TCP.

nodes.label: HTTP version model
nodes.description: A version is identified as HTTP/# according to the source.

nodes.label: TCP
nodes.description: Transmission Control Protocol used by HTTP before HTTP/3 and for HTTP/1.x and HTTP/2.

nodes.label: UDP
nodes.description: User Datagram Protocol used as the transport substrate for QUIC and by HTTP/3.

nodes.label: QUIC
nodes.description: Transport used by HTTP/3; provides reliability over UDP.

nodes.label: Reliable transport
nodes.description: Transport reliability required by HTTP's normal data exchange model.

nodes.label: TLS
nodes.description: Transport Layer Security used for encrypted HTTP connections and HTTP/2 deployment.

nodes.label: HTTPS
nodes.description: Secure variant of HTTP using encrypted HTTP connections.

nodes.label: ALPN
nodes.description: Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation extension used with TLS to negotiate HTTP versions/protocols.

nodes.label: Head-of-line blocking
nodes.description: Blocking phenomenon discussed for TCP streams and HTTP multiplexing.

nodes.label: Bidirectional streams
nodes.description: Multiple bidirectional streams within an HTTP/2 TCP connection.

nodes.label: Multiplexing
nodes.description: Concurrent HTTP requests/responses carried through shared connection resources.

nodes.label: Binary representation
nodes.description: HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 use binary protocol representations.

nodes.label: HPACK
nodes.description: Header compression mechanism for HTTP/2.

nodes.label: QPACK
nodes.description: Header compression mechanism for HTTP/3.

nodes.label: Server push
nodes.description: HTTP/2 capability for server applications to send data without periodic client polling.

nodes.label: HTTP connection
nodes.description: Real or virtual connection established between client and server for HTTP exchange.

nodes.label: Port 80
nodes.description: Typical port for unencrypted HTTP.

nodes.label: Port 443
nodes.description: Typical port for encrypted HTTP/HTTPS.

nodes.label: TCP 3-way handshake
nodes.description: TCP connection establishment overhead avoided on reused persistent connections.

nodes.label: TCP slow start
nodes.description: TCP mechanism referenced as contributing to connection performance over time.

nodes.label: HTTP keep-alive
nodes.description: HTTP/1.1 mechanism allowing connection reuse across multiple request/response pairs.

nodes.label: HTTP pipelining
nodes.description: HTTP/1.1 optimization allowing multiple requests before waiting for responses; later removed from most browsers.

nodes.label: TCP connection congestion
nodes.description: TCP congestion can temporarily block or slow data flow across streams.

nodes.label: HTTP message
nodes.description: At highest level, an HTTP message consists of a header followed by an optional body.

nodes.label: HTTP header
nodes.description: Header metadata associated with an HTTP message.

nodes.label: HTTP body
nodes.description: Optional data portion of an HTTP message.

nodes.label: Start line
nodes.description: Structured first line whose form differs between request and response.

nodes.label: Header fields
nodes.description: Zero or more header-field lines in HTTP/1.1, with Host required in requests.

nodes.label: Empty line
nodes.description: Blank line marking end of HTTP/1.1 headers.

nodes.label: CRLF
nodes.description: Carriage-return and line-feed sequence terminating HTTP/1.1 header lines.

nodes.label: ASCII
nodes.description: Encoding used by HTTP/1.1 header lines.

nodes.label: Content-Type
nodes.description: Header specifying Internet media type of conveyed data.

nodes.label: Content-Length
nodes.description: Header specifying body length in bytes when known.

nodes.label: Content-Encoding
nodes.description: Header specifying content compression/encoding such as gzip.

nodes.label: Transfer-Encoding
nodes.description: HTTP/1.1 header that can indicate chunked transfer encoding.

nodes.label: ETag
nodes.description: Entity tag used to determine whether cached content matches current server content.

nodes.label: Last-Modified
nodes.description: Header describing last modification time of a resource.

nodes.label: Accept-Ranges
nodes.description: Header indicating server support for byte-range requests.

nodes.label: Connection close
nodes.description: Header value indicating the server will close the TCP connection after transfer.

nodes.label: Host
nodes.description: Request header distinguishing DNS names sharing an IP address and enabling name-based virtual hosting.

nodes.label: User-Agent
nodes.description: Header identifying client software/user-agent information.

nodes.label: Accept-Language
nodes.description: Example request header indicating preferred languages.

nodes.label: Accept-Encoding
nodes.description: Example request header indicating supported content encodings.

nodes.label: Cookie
nodes.description: HTTP header mechanism associated with application/session state and client identification.

nodes.label: HTTP Referer
nodes.description: Header listed in the source's metadata/header field examples.

nodes.label: DNT
nodes.description: Do-Not-Track header example.

nodes.label: X-Forwarded-For
nodes.description: Header listed among HTTP header fields.

nodes.label: Global Privacy Control
nodes.description: Privacy-related signal referenced as a header-field example.

nodes.label: GET
nodes.description: retrieve a representation of a resource without intended server-state modification

nodes.label: HEAD
nodes.description: like GET but without representation data in the response body

nodes.label: POST
nodes.description: process a resource in some way

nodes.label: PUT
nodes.description: create or update a resource using the state supplied in the request

nodes.label: DELETE
nodes.description: delete a resource

nodes.label: CONNECT
nodes.description: ask an intermediary to establish a TCP/IP tunnel to an origin server

nodes.label: OPTIONS
nodes.description: request information about methods supported for a resource

nodes.label: TRACE
nodes.description: ask the server to return the received request in the response body for debugging

nodes.label: PATCH
nodes.description: modify a resource according to partial state in the request

nodes.label: QUERY
nodes.description: process enclosed content safely/idempotently and return the result

nodes.label: Safe method
nodes.description: A method whose request has no intended effect on server state; source defines GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE, QUERY as safe.

nodes.label: Idempotent method
nodes.description: A method for which multiple identical requests have the same effect as one such request.

nodes.label: Cacheable method
nodes.description: A method whose responses may be stored for future reuse.

nodes.label: Method name
nodes.description: HTTP method names are case-sensitive.

nodes.label: Method RFC mapping
nodes.description: Source table mapping methods to RFCs and payload/safety/idempotence/cacheability properties.

nodes.label: Request URI
nodes.description: URI identifying the target resource in an HTTP request.

nodes.label: Resource state
nodes.description: State associated with a resource and modified by state-changing methods.

nodes.label: Resource representation
nodes.description: Representation of a resource requested by methods such as GET.

nodes.label: Dynamic resource
nodes.description: Resource whose content is generated dynamically by server execution.

nodes.label: File resource
nodes.description: Common implementation of a server resource.

nodes.label: Executable output
nodes.description: Output of an executable running on the server can constitute a resource.

nodes.label: Query string
nodes.description: URL query component relevant to safe/idempotent GET usage examples.

nodes.label: Name-based virtual hosting
nodes.description: Hosting multiple DNS names on a shared IP distinguished by Host.

nodes.label: DNS name
nodes.description: DNS hostname carried in Host for virtual hosting.

nodes.label: HTTP status code
nodes.description: Three-digit decimal integer describing the disposition of a server attempt to satisfy a request.

nodes.label: Reason phrase
nodes.description: Human-readable phrase associated with a response status; standard phrases are recommendations.

nodes.label: 1xx Informational
nodes.description: Request received; processing continues.

nodes.label: 2xx Successful
nodes.description: Request successfully received, understood, and accepted.

nodes.label: 3xx Redirection
nodes.description: Further action is needed to complete the request.

nodes.label: 4xx Client Error
nodes.description: Request cannot be fulfilled due to an issue the client might control.

nodes.label: 5xx Server Error
nodes.description: Server failed to fulfill an apparently valid request.

formal_models.name: Resource addressing model
formal_models.meaning: Resources are identified through URI/URL and represented in messages.

formal_models.name: HTTP/1.1 message model
formal_models.expression: start-line + header-fields + CRLF delimiter + optional body
formal_models.meaning: HTTP/1.1 message structure described in the source.

formal_models.name: HTTP/2 multiplexing model
formal_models.expression: one TCP/IP connection -> multiple bidirectional streams -> concurrent requests/responses
formal_models.meaning: HTTP/2 shares a connection across streams.

formal_models.name: HTTP/3 transport model
formal_models.meaning: HTTP/3 replaces TCP transport with QUIC over UDP.

formal_models.name: Caching model
formal_models.expression: request -> cache lookup -> reuse or conditional retrieval -> response
formal_models.meaning: Caches and conditional requests reduce repeated network transfer.

formal_models.name: HTTP authentication model
formal_models.expression: server challenge -> client credentials -> access decision

formal_models.name: Status classification model
formal_models.meaning: Response disposition is classified by status-code class.

formal_models.name: Method semantics model
formal_models.expression: method -> intended action + safety + idempotence + cacheability
formal_models.meaning: HTTP methods have defined semantic properties.

formal_models.name: Persistent connection model
formal_models.expression: one TCP connection -> multiple HTTP requests/responses
formal_models.meaning: HTTP/1.1 keep-alive reduces repeated TCP setup.

formal_models.name: Range retrieval model
formal_models.meaning: Byte serving retrieves selected portions and can resume interrupted downloads.

formal_models.name: Application session model
formal_models.expression: stateless HTTP + cookie/hidden variable/etc. -> application session
formal_models.meaning: Sessions are implemented above HTTP's stateless protocol semantics.

source_claims.statement: HTTP is an application-layer protocol in the Internet protocol suite for distributed, collaborative hypermedia information systems.
HTTP is foundational to World Wide Web data communication.
HTTP uses request-response in the client-server model.
Browsers, crawlers, voice browsers, mobile apps and other software can act as user agents.
HTTP supports intermediate caches and proxies; some headers are hop-by-hop and others end-to-end.
Web resources are located through URL/URI schemes http and https.
HTTP/0.9, 1.0, 1.1, 2 and 3 are the versions listed with their introduction years/statuses.
HTTP/1.0 used a separate TCP connection per resource; HTTP/1.1 introduced reusable persistent connections.
HTTP/2 adds binary header representation, multiplexed streams, and server push.
HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP rather than TCP.
HTTP data exchange uses reliable transport; TCP is the pre-HTTP/3 standard choice.
HTTP/1.1 messages have start line, header fields, blank line, and optional body.
HTTP methods classify requested actions and have safety, idempotence, and cacheability properties.
GET is intended to retrieve without modifying server state, while other methods can modify state.
Safe methods are GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE and QUERY in the supplied source.
Idempotent methods include PUT, DELETE and safe methods; POST, CONNECT and PATCH are not necessarily idempotent.
GET, HEAD and POST are defined as cacheable in the source table.
HTTP response status codes are three-digit classes 1xx through 5xx.
HTTP is stateless; application sessions can be implemented with cookies, hidden variables or other mechanisms.
HTTP provides Basic and Digest authentication through challenge-response.
HTTPS is the popular encrypted form of HTTP.
HTTP/1.1 message headers use ASCII lines terminated by CRLF.
HTTP/1.1 supports conditional retrieval, chunked transfer and byte-range serving.
Tim Berners-Lee and CERN are credited with HTTP's invention/development.
HTTP/0.9 supported only GET and returned HTML pages.
SPDY influenced HTTP/2 and was developed by Google.
HTTP/2 was published in 2015 and HTTP/3 was standardized in 2022.
RFC 9110/9111/9112/9113/9114 are the current semantic/caching/version documents listed by the source.

semantic_distinctions.difference: HTTPS is the secure variant of HTTP.
HTTP/1.1 supports reusable persistent connections; HTTP/1.0 normally closed after response.
HTTP/2 uses binary framing and multiplexed streams rather than HTTP/1.1's textual message exchange.
HTTP/2 uses TCP; HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP.
Hop-by-hop headers can be managed by intermediaries; end-to-end headers are managed only by endpoints.
Safe means no intended server-state effect; idempotent means repeated identical requests have the same intended effect.
Cacheability is whether responses may be stored; it is distinct from safety.
GET retrieves a representation and is safe/cacheable; POST processes a resource and is not safe/idempotent by definition.
PUT supplies state for create/update at client-specified target; PATCH applies partial state.
HTTP authentication belongs to protocol access control; application login/session is application-level.
A resource is the target concept; a representation is the data form returned for it.
Header names are case-insensitive; method names are case-sensitive.
Status codes are machine-readable; reason phrases are human-readable recommendations.
Persistent reuse keeps a connection open; pipelining sends multiple requests before responses and had interoperability problems.
Chunked transfer supports unknown-length streaming; Content-Length explicitly states known length.
Byte ranges retrieve only selected portions.
TCP is the traditional reliable transport; QUIC provides reliability over UDP for HTTP/3.
HTTP/0.9 was extremely minimal, with only GET and HTML responses.
SPDY was an alternative Google protocol whose ideas influenced HTTP/2.
The source describes HTTP as displacing Gopher for content delivery in the early 1990s.

misconceptions.misconception: HTTP itself is TCP.
misconceptions.correction: HTTP is an application protocol; TCP is a traditional underlying transport, while HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP.

misconceptions.misconception: HTTP/3 is just HTTP/2 with a different version number.
misconceptions.correction: HTTP/3 changes the transport model to QUIC over UDP.

misconceptions.misconception: HTTP is stateful because websites have logins.
misconceptions.correction: HTTP itself is stateless; application sessions add state above HTTP.

misconceptions.misconception: Safe means idempotent and idempotent means safe.
misconceptions.correction: They overlap for several methods but describe different semantic properties.

misconceptions.misconception: GET can never cause side effects.
misconceptions.correction: The source says implementations can misuse GET; safe describes intended semantics, not technical enforcement.

misconceptions.misconception: POST is idempotent.
misconceptions.correction: The source explicitly says POST is not necessarily idempotent.

misconceptions.misconception: All HTTP methods are cacheable.
misconceptions.correction: The source defines only GET, HEAD and POST as cacheable.

misconceptions.misconception: HTTP/1.1 always opens a new TCP connection for every resource.
misconceptions.correction: HTTP/1.1 can reuse persistent connections.

misconceptions.misconception: HTTP/2 sends multiple independent TCP connections for every request.
misconceptions.correction: The source describes multiplexed streams over a shared TCP/IP connection.

misconceptions.misconception: HTTP/3 uses TCP underneath QUIC.
misconceptions.correction: QUIC runs over UDP.

misconceptions.misconception: Header field names and method names use the same case rules.
misconceptions.correction: Methods are case-sensitive; header field names are case-insensitive.

misconceptions.misconception: A response body is always present.
misconceptions.correction: The body is optional.

misconceptions.misconception: A resource is always a static file.
misconceptions.correction: The source says resources may be files or dynamically generated/executable output.

misconceptions.misconception: Authentication and application login are the same HTTP mechanism.
misconceptions.correction: The source distinguishes HTTP authentication from application-session login.

misconceptions.misconception: HTTP/0.9 supported POST and arbitrary content formats.
misconceptions.correction: The source says HTTP/0.9 supported only GET and returned HTML pages.

misconceptions.misconception: HTTP/2 made HTTP/1.1 obsolete.
misconceptions.correction: The source describes HTTP/2 as an evolution while HTTP/1.1 remains a standard version.

misconceptions.misconception: HTTPS is a different application protocol unrelated to HTTP.
misconceptions.correction: HTTPS is described as the secure variant of HTTP.

misconceptions.misconception: Byte-range serving always downloads the whole resource.
misconceptions.correction: It retrieves selected portions and can resume interrupted downloads.

misconceptions.misconception: Chunked transfer requires Content-Length.
misconceptions.correction: Chunked transfer is specifically useful when length is not known in advance.

misconceptions.misconception: Status reason phrases are the machine-readable part of responses.
misconceptions.correction: Status codes are machine-readable; reason phrases are human-readable.

historical_context.description: Source says Berners-Lee proposed the WorldWideWeb project in 1989.
Source says the first web server went live in 1990.
First documented official HTTP version, supporting only GET and HTML retrieval.
RFC 2068 officially released HTTP/1.1 in January 1997.
Google announced SPDY as a binary protocol for faster web traffic.
HTTP/2 published in May 2015 as RFC 7540.
HTTP/3 standardized by IETF as RFC 9114 on 6 June 2022.
HTTP semantics/caching/version documents were refactored into RFC 9110-9114 family.
